name: Silbo Gomero whistled language
lineage: Silbo Gomero whistled-language tradition of La Gomera island, Canary Islands — a fully grammatical whistled register of the Spanish language using turbulent lip-and-tongue-formed source (no vocal-fold vibration, distinct from the M3 whistle vocal register) to encode vowels and consonants across the mountain-canyon distances of the island terrain (sound carries 2-5 km across canyon walls); whistled vowels mapped onto two pitches (high and low) and whistled consonants mapped onto two-and-more types of pitch-transition (interrupted vs continuous, with rising vs falling), giving sufficient phonemic-distinction-capacity to transmit any Spanish-language utterance; preserved through the La Gomera school curriculum (1999-onward compulsory instruction) and the ethnographic lineage of Ramón Trujillo who established the linguistic-phonological description in the 1970s-80s; parallel related whistled-language traditions include Sfyria (Antia village Greek), Mazatec (Oaxaca Mexico), Kuşköy (Turkish Black Sea), and the Hmong courtship-whistle traditions
